The number of teachers per school ranged from 1 to 25, with an average of 14.41 teachers per school (Median = 15.5). This indicates a hierarchical data structure where teachers are nested within schools.


In this study, a two-level hierarchical structure is employed, in which teachers (Level 1) are nested within schools (Level 2). A subset of variables from the PISA 2022 Teacher and School Questionnaires is selected to investigate how individual teacher characteristics and school-level factors are associated with teacher outcomes. The analysis sample is restricted to teachers with valid observations on the variables included in the respective models.

The main dependent variable is teachers' overall job satisfaction (TC258Q01JA), measured on a 0–10 scale, where higher values indicate greater job satisfaction. The extension analysis uses a binary dependent variable based on whether teachers have seriously considered leaving classroom teaching (TC250Q01JA).

A total of seven predictors are included and used consistently across both models. At the individual level (Level 1), the predictors include teacher age (TC002Q01NA), total teaching experience (TC007Q02NA), weekly working hours (TC215Q01JA), use of ICT in teaching (TC169Q11HA), and perceived work-related stress (TC254Q01JA). Age, teaching experience, and weekly working hours are numerical variables, whereas ICT use and perceived work-related stress are measured on ordinal response scales. These variables are obtained from the Teacher Questionnaire and vary across teachers within schools.

At the school level (Level 2), the predictors include lack of respect for teachers among students (SC061Q03TA), measured as the extent to which students' lack of respect for teachers is perceived to hinder learning in the school, and the proportion of students from socioeconomically disadvantaged homes (SC211Q03JA). The latter is measured as a percentage. These variables are obtained from the School Questionnaire and are constant for all teachers within the same school.

Multilevel models with random intercepts are estimated to account for the clustering of teachers within schools. In addition, random-slope models for perceived work-related stress are tested to examine whether the association between stress and job satisfaction varies across schools. The ordinal predictor variables are treated as numerical covariates in the models.

## Introducing Variables and Descriptive Analysis


```{r,results='markup'}

# Check possible ID variables
names(tch)[grepl("TCH|TEACH|ID", names(tch), ignore.case = TRUE)]

# Create a unique row ID for each teacher, then merge teacher and school data
data <- tch %>%
  mutate(teacher_id = row_number()) %>%
  left_join(sch, by = "CNTSCHID")

# Select variables, rename them, and remove missing values
data_model <- data %>%
  transmute(
    school_id = CNTSCHID,
    teacher_id = teacher_id,
    original_teacher_id = CNTTCHID,
    
    # Dependent variables
    satisfaction = TC258Q01JA,
    leave = case_when(
      TC250Q01JA == 1 ~ 1,
      TC250Q01JA == 2 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    
    # Level 1 predictors
    age = TC002Q01NA,
    experience = TC007Q02NA,
    working_hours = TC215Q01JA,
    ict_use = TC169Q11HA,
    stress = TC254Q01JA,
    
    # Level 2 predictors from school questionnaire
    lack_of_respect = SC061Q03TA,
    ses_disadvantage = SC211Q03JA
  ) %>%
  na.omit()

# Check raw data
summary(data_model)
dim(data_model)
length(unique(data_model$school_id))

# Show teachers with highest working hours
data_model %>%
  arrange(desc(working_hours)) %>%
  dplyr::select(teacher_id, original_teacher_id, school_id, working_hours) %>%
  head(30)

summary(data_model)

nrow(data)
nrow(data_model)
nrow(data) - nrow(data_model)
```

## Descriptive Statistics and Data Preparation


The analytical dataset was constructed by merging the PISA 2022 Teacher
and School Questionnaires using the school identifier. The analysis was
restricted to observations with complete information on the variables
included in the models. The resulting dataset contained `r nrow(data_model)` teachers
nested within `r length(unique(data_model$school_id))` schools before the additional screening of weekly
working hours. The complete-case procedure excluded `r nrow(data) - nrow(data_model)` observations due
to missing information.

The main continuous outcome was teacher job satisfaction (TC258Q01JA), 
which is measured on a 0-10 scale, with higher values indicating greater 
job satisfaction. The binary extension outcome was constructed from 
TC250Q01JA, where a value of 1 indicates that the teacher had seriously 
considered leaving classroom teaching and a value of 0 indicates that the 
teacher had not.

The teacher-level predictors were age, teaching experience, weekly 
working hours, ICT use, and perceived work-related stress. The school-level 
predictors were lack of respect for teachers among students and the 
proportion of students from socioeconomically disadvantaged homes. These 
variables correspond to the teacher- and school-level variables specified 
in the research design. 

Weekly working hours required additional data screening. The initial 
distribution contained implausibly large values, including a reported 
value of 3,600 hours per week. To identify extreme observations 
systematically, an IQR-based rule was applied. Observations below 
12.5 hours or above 72.5 hours per week were classified as outliers and 
excluded from the analysis. After this procedure, weekly working hours 
ranged from 13 to 72 hours per week. This screening step was performed 
before fitting the multilevel models in order to reduce the influence of 
implausible observations on the estimated coefficients. 


```{r,results='markup'}

# IQR-based outlier thresholds for working hours
Q1 <- quantile(data_model$working_hours, 0.25)
Q3 <- quantile(data_model$working_hours, 0.75)
IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1

lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_val
upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_val

# Before cleaning plots
hist(data_model$working_hours,
     breaks = 50,
     main = "Before Cleaning: Histogram",
     xlab = "Working Hours",
     col = "lightblue")

boxplot(data_model$working_hours,
        main = "Before Cleaning: Boxplot",
        col = "lightblue")

# Remove outliers
data_model_clean <- data_model %>%
  filter(working_hours >= lower_bound,
         working_hours <= upper_bound)

lower_bound
upper_bound

# After cleaning plots
hist(data_model_clean$working_hours,
     breaks = 30,
     main = "After Cleaning: Histogram",
     xlab = "Working Hours",
     col = "lightgreen")

boxplot(data_model_clean$working_hours,
        main = "After Cleaning: Boxplot",
        col = "lightgreen")

summary(data_model_clean$working_hours)

```

The IQR-based outlier detection procedure identified several extreme observations for weekly working hours. In particular, values such as 3,600 hours per week were clearly implausible and likely resulted from reporting or coding errors. Outliers were defined as observations falling below 12.5 hours or above 72.5 hours per week (Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, respectively). After excluding these observations, the distribution of working hours became more symmetric and concentrated around its central tendency, with values ranging from 13 to 72 hours per week. This cleaning procedure improved the plausibility of the variable and reduced the potential influence of extreme observations on the estimation of the multilevel models.


```{r,results='markup'}

data_model_clean <- data_model_clean %>%
  mutate(
    age_z = as.numeric(scale(age)),
    experience_z = as.numeric(scale(experience)),
    working_hours_z = as.numeric(scale(working_hours)),
    ict_use_z = as.numeric(scale(ict_use)),
    stress_z = as.numeric(scale(stress)),
    lack_of_respect_z = as.numeric(scale(lack_of_respect)),
    ses_disadvantage_z = as.numeric(scale(ses_disadvantage))
  )

summary(data_model_clean)
 
```

I standardized all continuous predictor variables (age, experience, working hours, ICT use, stress, lack of respect, and socioeconomic disadvantage) by transforming them into z-scores before fitting the multilevel model. Standardization was performed by subtracting the mean from each observation and dividing by the standard deviation of the respective variable, resulting in variables with a mean of approximately 0 and a standard deviation of 1. This procedure places all predictors on a common scale, allowing the regression coefficients to be directly compared in terms of their relative effects on teacher satisfaction. In addition, standardization helps improve numerical stability and reduces the risk of convergence problems during model estimation, particularly when predictors are measured on substantially different scales. After standardization, I converted the variables to numeric vectors to ensure compatibility with the mixed-effects modelling functions and to avoid potential issues caused by the matrix output generated by the scale() function.

## Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)

Prior to estimating the explanatory multilevel models, a null (empty) model was fitted to examine whether a meaningful proportion of variance in teacher job satisfaction was attributable to differences between schools. In order to estimate the ICC, the unconditional mean model is assumed:  
$$ \text{satisfaction}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j} + \varepsilon_{ij} $$  
In this model, the observed job satisfaction score ($\text{satisfaction}_{ij}$) for teacher $i$ in school $j$ is decomposed into specific structural components: 

$\gamma_{00}$: The overall (grand) average teacher job satisfaction across all schools in the population. 

$u_{0j}$: The school-specific random intercept, representing the deviation of school $j$'s average satisfaction from the grand mean ($\gamma_{00}$). It is assumed to be normally distributed, $u_{0j} \sim N(0, \sigma_{u_0}^2)$. 

$\varepsilon_{ij}$: The teacher-level residual error, representing individual differences in job satisfaction among teachers within the same school, assumed to be normally distributed, $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$.  The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is then defined based on these variance components:  

$$ \text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma_{u_0}^2}{\sigma_{u_0}^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2} $$  
where $\sigma_{u_0}^2$ represents the between-school variance (quantifying how much schools differ from one another in average teacher satisfaction) and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ represents the within-school residual variance (quantifying individual variation among teachers within the same school).

```{r,results='markup'}

# ICC: empty random-intercept model
# y_ij = gamma_00 + u_0j + e_ij

mod0 <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~ 1 + (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE
)

# Variance components
covrand <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(mod0))

sigma_school <- covrand[covrand$grp == "school_id", "vcov"]
sigma_resid  <- attr(VarCorr(mod0), "sc")^2

sigma_school
sigma_resid

# ICC
ICC_school <- sigma_school / (sigma_school + sigma_resid)

ICC_school

ICC_school*100 #percentage

```

Prior to estimating the explanatory multilevel models, a null (empty) model was fitted to examine whether a meaningful proportion of variance in teacher job satisfaction was attributable to differences between schools. The null model included only a fixed intercept and a random intercept for schools:

$$
y_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

where $y_{ij}$ denotes the job satisfaction score of teacher $i$ in school $j$, $\gamma_{00}$ is the overall mean job satisfaction, $u_{0j}$ is the school-specific random intercept, and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the teacher-level residual.


The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated as

$$
ICC =
\frac{\sigma^2_{u_0}}
{\sigma^2_{u_0}+\sigma^2_{\varepsilon}},
$$

where $\sigma^2_{u_0}$ denotes the between-school variance and
$\sigma^2_{\varepsilon}$ denotes the within-school residual variance.

The estimated ICC was $0.0106$, indicating that approximately $1.06\%$
of the total variance in teacher job satisfaction was attributable to
differences between schools, while approximately $98.94\%$ was
attributable to differences between teachers within schools. Thus, most
of the variation in teacher job satisfaction occurred at the teacher
level, with relatively little variation attributable to differences
between schools.

Despite the relatively small ICC, a multilevel modelling framework was
retained because teachers are nested within schools, meaning that
observations from the same school may not be statistically independent.
Moreover, the analysis includes school-level predictors, which require
the hierarchical structure to be explicitly represented in the model.
The multilevel framework therefore accounts for the clustering of
teachers within schools while allowing school-level characteristics to
be included as predictors of teacher job satisfaction.


## Model Specification

### Level 1 Model (Teacher Level)

$$
satisfaction_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\text{age\_z}_{ij} + \beta_{2j}\text{experience\_z}_{ij} + \beta_{3j}\text{working\_hours\_z}_{ij} + \beta_{4j}\text{ict\_use\_z}_{ij} + \beta_{5j}\text{stress\_z}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

where 
$$
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

### Level 2 Model (School Level)

$$
\beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\text{lack\_of\_respect\_z}_{j} + \gamma_{02}\text{ses\_disadvantage\_z}_{j} + u_{0j}
$$

where
$$
u_{0j} \sim N(0, \sigma_{u_0}^2)
$$

In this starting specification the five teacher-level slopes are fixed
(no random-slope terms yet), so each Level-1 coefficient is replaced by
a single Level-2 parameter:

$$
\beta_{1j}=\gamma_{10},\quad
\beta_{2j}=\gamma_{20},\quad
\beta_{3j}=\gamma_{30},\quad
\beta_{4j}=\gamma_{40},\quad
\beta_{5j}=\gamma_{50}.
$$

Which of these slopes should instead be allowed to vary across schools
(i.e. written as $\beta_{pj}=\gamma_{p0}+u_{pj}$) is exactly what the
Random Slope Test below decides. Because every fixed effect in the
combined model is a Level-2 parameter, all fixed-effect hypotheses in
this report are stated in terms of $\gamma$ rather than $\beta$.

### Combined Model

$$
satisfaction_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{10}\text{age\_z}_{ij} + \gamma_{20}\text{experience\_z}_{ij} + \gamma_{30}\text{working\_hours\_z}_{ij} + \gamma_{40}\text{ict\_use\_z}_{ij} + \gamma_{50}\text{stress\_z}_{ij} + \gamma_{01}\text{lack\_of\_respect\_z}_{j} + \gamma_{02}\text{ses\_disadvantage\_z}_{j} + u_{0j} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$



### Fixed Effects

This is the *saturated* starting specification, from which the modeling
strategy described later (random effects tested first, then fixed
effects by backward elimination) proceeds. It includes the following
fixed effects:

- Overall intercept ($\gamma_{00}$)
- Teacher age ($\gamma_{10}$)
- Teaching experience ($\gamma_{20}$)
- Weekly working hours ($\gamma_{30}$)
- ICT use ($\gamma_{40}$)
- Stress ($\gamma_{50}$)
- Lack of respect at the school level ($\gamma_{01}$)
- Socioeconomic disadvantage at the school level ($\gamma_{02}$)

Two of these ($\gamma_{30}$ and $\gamma_{02}$) are removed during the
Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection reported below; the final model
therefore contains five fixed-effect predictors rather than seven.

### Random Effects

The model includes one random effect:

- School-specific random intercept ($u_{0j}$), where $u_{0j} \sim N(0, \sigma_{u_0}^2)$

### Residual Error

The teacher-level residual error is:

$$
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)
$$

which captures unexplained variation between teachers within the same school.

## Random Effects Test


```{r,results='markup'}

# Random-intercept model (ML estimation, needed for the LRT below)
# Note: this is a separate object from the REML-estimated mod0 used
# above for the ICC, since LRTs on fixed/random effects require ML.
mod0_ml <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~ 1 + (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = FALSE
)

# Single-level model without random intercept
mod0a <- lm(
  satisfaction ~ 1,
  data = data_model_clean
)

# Likelihood-ratio test
test0 <- anova(mod0_ml, mod0a, refit = FALSE)

test0

LL0 <- test0$Chisq[2]

p_corrected <- 0.5 * pchisq(LL0, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

p_corrected

VarCorr(mod0_ml)
```

### Random Effects Test: Results

To determine whether a school-level random intercept was required, a likelihood ratio test (LRT) was conducted. The random-intercept model was compared with a single-level model that did not include any school-level random effects.

The hypotheses were:

$$
H_0:\quad \sigma^2_{u_0} = 0
$$


$$
H_A:\quad \sigma^2_{u_0} > 0
$$

Here, (u_{0j}) represents the school-specific random intercept, and (\sigma^2_{u_0}) denotes the variance of the random intercept across schools.

### Comparison of the Random-Intercept and Single-Level Models

To assess whether teacher job satisfaction varies systematically across
schools, an empty random-intercept model was compared with a corresponding
single-level model containing only a fixed intercept. Both models were
estimated using maximum likelihood.

The likelihood-ratio test comparing the random-intercept model with the
single-level model yielded $\chi^2(1)=1.65$ and an uncorrected
$p=.1994$. Because the null hypothesis places the random-intercept
variance on the boundary of the parameter space
($\sigma^2_{u0}=0$), the usual chi-square reference distribution is not
directly applicable. Following the boundary correction, the p-value was
calculated as one half of the conventional chi-square tail probability,
resulting in a corrected $p=.100$.

Thus, at the conventional 5\% significance level, the null hypothesis
that the between-school variance is zero was not rejected. There is
therefore insufficient evidence that including a school-specific random
intercept significantly improves the fit of the unconditional job
satisfaction model.

The information criteria led to a similar conclusion. The AIC was
10668 for both the single-level and random-intercept models, indicating
virtually no difference in relative model fit. The BIC was 10680 for the
single-level model and 10686 for the random-intercept model. Because lower
values indicate better relative fit, the BIC slightly favored the simpler
single-level model.

The estimated standard deviation of the school-specific random intercept
was $SD=0.189$, while the residual standard deviation was $SD=1.873$.
Overall, these results suggest that there is relatively little evidence
of substantial between-school variation in teacher job satisfaction in the
unconditional model.



## Random Slope Test

 1. Individual Random Slope Tests
For each predictor $v$ (where $v \in \{\text{age\_z}, \text{experience\_z}, \text{working\_hours\_z}, \text{ict\_use\_z}, \text{stress\_z}\}$), the baseline random intercept model is compared against a model incorporating a random slope.

Age Random Slope (`age_z`):
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{age}} = 0$ (The effect of teacher age on job satisfaction does not vary across schools)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{age}} > 0$ (The effect of teacher age on job satisfaction varies significantly across schools)

Experience Random Slope (`experience_z`):
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{exp}} = 0$ (The effect of teaching experience on job satisfaction does not vary across schools)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{exp}} > 0$ (The effect of teaching experience on job satisfaction varies significantly across schools)

Working Hours Random Slope (`working_hours_z`):
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{hours}} = 0$ (The effect of working hours on job satisfaction does not vary across schools)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{hours}} > 0$ (The effect of working hours on job satisfaction varies significantly across schools)

ICT Use Random Slope (`ict_use_z`):
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{ict}} = 0$ (The effect of ICT use on job satisfaction does not vary across schools)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{ict}} > 0$ (The effect of ICT use on job satisfaction varies significantly across schools)

Stress Random Slope (`stress_z`):
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{stress}} = 0$ (The effect of job stress on job satisfaction does not vary across schools)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{stress}} > 0$ (The effect of job stress on job satisfaction varies significantly across schools)



#### 2. Uncorrelated Random Slope Test for Stress (`mod_stress_uncorr`)
This test compares the random intercept model with an uncorrelated random slope model for stress (`(1 + stress_z || school_id)`), constraining the covariance between the intercept and slope to zero ($\rho = 0$).

Hypothesis:
$H_0: \sigma^2_{1,\text{stress}} = 0 \quad (\text{with } \rho = 0)$ (The variance of the stress slope is zero, and the random-intercept-only model is sufficient)
$H_1: \sigma^2_{1,\text{stress}} > 0 \quad (\text{with } \rho = 0)$ (The effect of stress varies across schools even when constraining the covariance to zero)

```{r,results='markup'}

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Random-intercept model (baseline for all random-slope tests)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
mod_ri_reml <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~
    age_z +
    experience_z +
    working_hours_z +
    ict_use_z +
    stress_z +
    lack_of_respect_z +
    ses_disadvantage_z +
    (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE   # REML for random-effects tests, per Session 3
)

# Predictors for which random slopes are tested
vars <- c(
  "age_z",
  "experience_z",
  "working_hours_z",
  "ict_use_z",
  "stress_z"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: correlated random-slope test for each predictor
# (adds both the slope variance and its covariance with the
# intercept at once, so the mixture correction is required
# rather than the raw p-value)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
for (v in vars) {

  form <- as.formula(
    paste0(
      "satisfaction ~ ",
      "age_z + experience_z + working_hours_z + ",
      "ict_use_z + stress_z + ",
      "lack_of_respect_z + ses_disadvantage_z + ",
      "(1 + ", v, " | school_id)"
    )
  )

  mod_rs <- lmer(
    form,
    data = data_model_clean,
    REML = TRUE   # REML for random-effects tests, per Session 3
  )

  test_v  <- anova(mod_ri_reml, mod_rs, refit = FALSE)
  chisq_v <- test_v$Chisq[2]

  # Mixture correction: 0.5 * chi-square(1) + 0.5 * chi-square(2)
  p_mixture_v <- 0.5 * pchisq(chisq_v, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) +
                 0.5 * pchisq(chisq_v, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

  cat("\n=== Random slope (correlated):", v, "===\n")
  print(test_v)
  cat("Mixture-corrected p-value:", p_mixture_v, "\n")
  cat("Singular fit:", isSingular(mod_rs), "\n")
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Step 2: stress random-slope models (H6, H7, H8)
# H6 = correlated random slope for stress vs. random-intercept-only
#      (fit as mod_stress below; also produced by the Step-1 loop
#      above when v = "stress_z", chi-sq(2) = 40.515)
# H7 = uncorrelated random slope for stress vs. random-intercept-only
#      (fit as mod_stress_uncorr below)
# H8 = covariance test, uncorrelated vs. correlated stress models
# ---------------------------------------------------------

# Correlated random intercept and random slope (H6)
mod_stress <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~
    age_z +
    experience_z +
    working_hours_z +
    ict_use_z +
    stress_z +
    lack_of_respect_z +
    ses_disadvantage_z +
    (1 + stress_z | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE   # REML for random-effects tests, per Session 3
)
isSingular(mod_stress)
VarCorr(mod_stress)

# Uncorrelated stress random-slope model (correlation fixed at 0)
mod_stress_uncorr <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~
    age_z +
    experience_z +
    working_hours_z +
    ict_use_z +
    stress_z +
    lack_of_respect_z +
    ses_disadvantage_z +
    (1 + stress_z || school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE   # REML for random-effects tests, per Session 3
)
isSingular(mod_stress_uncorr)
VarCorr(mod_stress_uncorr)

# H7: single-parameter test of the stress slope variance
# (uncorrelated specification; boundary correction: p/2)
test_stress_uncorr <- anova(mod_ri_reml, mod_stress_uncorr, refit = FALSE)
chisq_stress <- test_stress_uncorr$Chisq[2]
p_stress_corrected <- 0.5 * pchisq(chisq_stress, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

test_stress_uncorr
cat("H7 boundary-corrected p-value:", p_stress_corrected, "\n")

# H8: covariance test (not a boundary parameter, so no
# correction is required)
covariance_LRT_continuous <- anova(mod_stress_uncorr, mod_stress, refit = FALSE)
covariance_LRT_continuous

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Step 3: does an ICT-use random slope survive ON TOP OF the
# already-retained stress random slope? H5 above only tested
# ICT's slope against the random-intercept-only model, so it
# never actually checked whether ICT's slope still holds once
# stress's slope is already in the model. This step resolves
# that directly instead of leaving it as an open note.
# ---------------------------------------------------------
mod_stress_ict_uncorr <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~
    age_z +
    experience_z +
    working_hours_z +
    ict_use_z +
    stress_z +
    lack_of_respect_z +
    ses_disadvantage_z +
    (1 + stress_z + ict_use_z || school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE   # REML for random-effects tests, per Session 3
)

isSingular(mod_stress_ict_uncorr)
mod_stress_ict_uncorr@optinfo$conv
VarCorr(mod_stress_ict_uncorr)

# Adding the ICT slope on top of the stress-only model adds a
# single boundary parameter (the ICT slope variance), so the
# same p/2 boundary correction as H7 applies here. This is H9.
test_stress_ict <- anova(mod_stress_uncorr, mod_stress_ict_uncorr, refit = FALSE)
chisq_stress_ict <- test_stress_ict$Chisq[2]
p_stress_ict_corrected <- 0.5 * pchisq(chisq_stress_ict, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

test_stress_ict
cat("ICT-slope-on-top-of-stress boundary-corrected p-value:", p_stress_ict_corrected, "\n")

# Decision rule: retain the ICT random slope in the final model
# only if it (a) significantly improves fit here and (b) is
# stable (non-singular, clean convergence). This is the same
# significance-and-stability rule used later for the logistic
# extension's automated model selection, applied consistently.
converged_lmm <- function(model) {
  conv <- model@optinfo$conv
  opt_ok  <- is.null(conv$opt) || conv$opt == 0
  lme4_ok <- is.null(conv$lme4$code)
  opt_ok && lme4_ok
}

ict_slope_retained <- !is.na(p_stress_ict_corrected) &&
  p_stress_ict_corrected < .05 &&
  !isSingular(mod_stress_ict_uncorr) &&
  converged_lmm(mod_stress_ict_uncorr)

cat("ICT random slope retained in final model:", ict_slope_retained, "\n")

# Random-effects part of the final model formula, built
# programmatically so the model fit later always matches this
# decision rather than being hardcoded independently of it.
final_re_formula <- if (ict_slope_retained) {
  "(1 + stress_z + ict_use_z || school_id)"
} else {
  "(1 + stress_z || school_id)"
}
```

### Random-Slope Model Selection

Random-slope models were estimated for age, teaching experience, weekly
working hours, ICT use, and perceived work-related stress. Each model
was compared with the random-intercept model using likelihood-ratio
tests under REML estimation, following the modeling strategy of Session 3
(random effects are tested with REML, fixed effects with ML). In R this
requires `anova(..., refit = FALSE)`, since `anova()` otherwise refits
both models with ML. Because each comparison adds
two parameters simultaneously — the slope variance and its covariance
with the random intercept — the raw likelihood-ratio p-value is not
appropriate on its own. Following the boundary-correction approach
described in the estimation lecture, a mixture-corrected p-value was
computed as $p = 0.5 \cdot P(\chi^2_1 > \text{obs}) + 0.5 \cdot P(\chi^2_2 > \text{obs})$
for each test.

The random slopes for age and teaching experience did not significantly
improve model fit, $\chi^2(2) = 2.34$, mixture-corrected $p = .218$, and
$\chi^2(2) = 2.08$, mixture-corrected $p = .251$, respectively; both
models were also singular. The random slope for weekly working hours
likewise did not significantly improve fit, $\chi^2(2) = 3.30$,
mixture-corrected $p = .131$, and this model was not singular.

The random-slope model for ICT use produced a significant
likelihood-ratio test, $\chi^2(2) = 14.43$, mixture-corrected
$p < .001$, and this model was **not** singular, indicating a stable
estimate of slope variance and covariance for this predictor.

The correlated random-slope model for perceived stress (H6) also
significantly improved model fit relative to the random-intercept
model, $\chi^2(2) = 40.92$, mixture-corrected $p < .001$. However, this
model resulted in a singular fit, with the estimated correlation between
the school-specific random intercept and the random slope for stress
reaching the boundary ($\widehat{\text{Corr}} = 1.00$). The estimated
standard deviations were $0.245$ for the random intercept, $0.330$ for
the random slope, and $1.577$ for the residual, confirming that the
correlated random-effects structure was unstable for this predictor.

To address the singularity, an uncorrelated random-slope model was
estimated for stress, using the specification
$(1 + \text{stress\_z} \,||\, \text{school\_id})$. This model converged
without a singular-fit warning ($\widehat{\sigma}_{u_0} = 0.170$,
$\widehat{\sigma}_{u_1} = 0.305$, $\widehat{\sigma}_\varepsilon =
1.590$). The uncorrelated random-slope model (H7) significantly
improved fit relative to the random-intercept model, $\chi^2(1) =
16.14$, boundary-corrected $p < .001$ ($p = 2.95 \times 10^{-5}$). The
REML AIC decreased from $9952.6$ for the random-intercept model to
$9938.5$ for the uncorrelated random-slope model.

The formal covariance test comparing the uncorrelated and correlated
stress models (H8) also indicated a significant improvement in fit for
the correlated specification, $\chi^2(1) = 24.78$, $p = 6.42 \times
10^{-7}$, no boundary correction required. This result should be
interpreted alongside the singularity evidence above: although the
covariance term is statistically significant, the correlated model's
boundary estimate ($\widehat{\text{Corr}} = 1.00$) indicates the
estimate is not reliable, so the significant covariance test does not
override the decision to retain the uncorrelated specification for
stress.

The results support allowing the effects of both ICT use and perceived
stress on job satisfaction to vary across schools when each is tested
on its own against the random-intercept model. However, H5 only tested
the ICT slope against the random-intercept-only model, not against a
model that already contains the retained stress random slope, so it
does not by itself establish whether ICT's slope should also appear in
the final specification. To resolve this directly, an additional
nested model was fit that adds an uncorrelated random slope for ICT
use on top of the already-retained stress random slope, specified as
`(1 + stress_z + ict_use_z || school_id)`. Comparing this model against
the stress-only uncorrelated model isolates the marginal contribution
of the ICT slope, adding a single boundary parameter, so the same p/2
boundary correction used for H7 applies (this test is H9):
$\chi^2(1) = `r round(chisq_stress_ict, 3)`$, boundary-corrected
$p `r ifelse(p_stress_ict_corrected < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", signif(p_stress_ict_corrected, 3)))`$.
This joint model `r ifelse(isSingular(mod_stress_ict_uncorr) || !converged_lmm(mod_stress_ict_uncorr), "did not fit stably (singular and/or non-converged), so it cannot be trusted even where the test above suggests an improvement", "converged cleanly with no singular-fit warning, so the two random slopes can be estimated jointly without a stability concern")`.

Based on this test, the ICT random slope
**`r ifelse(ict_slope_retained, "is retained", "is not retained")`**
in the final model below. `r ifelse(ict_slope_retained, "Both the stress and ICT-use slopes are specified as uncorrelated with the random intercept and with each other, matching the stable specification already established for stress alone.", "Although ICT's slope was significant and stable when tested in isolation (H5), it does not survive as a stable, independent addition once the stress random slope is already present, so the final specification keeps only the uncorrelated random slope for stress. This is a scope decision resolved by an explicit test, not an unaddressed gap.")`


## Fixed Effects Test

```{r,results='markup'}

# Reduced model: random intercept only
m_reduced <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~ 1 +
    (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = FALSE
)

# Full fixed effects model with random intercept
m_fixed <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~
    age_z +
    experience_z +
    working_hours_z +
    ict_use_z +
    stress_z +
    lack_of_respect_z +
    ses_disadvantage_z +
    (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = FALSE
)


# Likelihood ratio test
anova(m_reduced, m_fixed)

summary(m_reduced)
summary(m_fixed)

```

To examine whether the predictor variables improved model fit, the
random-intercept-only model was compared with a model including all
teacher-level and school-level predictors using a likelihood-ratio test
(LRT). The full model included age, teaching experience, weekly working
hours, ICT use, perceived stress, lack of respect for teachers, and the
proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged students.

The hypotheses were:

$$
H_0:\quad
\gamma_{10}=\gamma_{20}=\gamma_{30}=\gamma_{40}=\gamma_{50}=\gamma_{01}=\gamma_{02}=0
$$

$$
H_A:
\text{At least one fixed-effect coefficient is not equal to zero.}
$$

Under the null hypothesis, none of the teacher-level or school-level
predictors contributes to explaining variation in teacher job
satisfaction. Under the alternative hypothesis, at least one predictor
is associated with teacher job satisfaction.

The likelihood-ratio test indicated that the full fixed-effects model
provided a substantially better fit to the data than the
random-intercept-only model, $\chi^2(7)=767.85$, $p<.001$. Therefore,
the null hypothesis was rejected, indicating that the predictors jointly
contributed to explaining variation in teacher job satisfaction.

This joint test (`m_fixed` vs. `m_reduced`, both random-intercept-only)
establishes that the predictor set as a whole improves fit; it is not
yet the model used for interpreting individual predictors. The
random-effects tests in the next section determine that the stress and
ICT-use slopes should be allowed to vary by school, and once those
random slopes are added the standard errors and degrees of freedom for
those two predictors change accordingly (most visibly for ICT use,
whose test is then based on only the schools' worth of residual
variation in that slope rather than the full teacher-level sample).
For that reason, the size, direction, and significance of each
individual predictor are reported and interpreted only once, in the
Final Model section below, using the model that includes those random
slopes -- not re-derived here from `m_fixed`, to avoid stating two
different numbers for the same coefficient in this document.

Because all predictors were standardized, the coefficients throughout
represent the expected change in teacher job satisfaction associated
with a one-standard-deviation increase in the corresponding predictor,
holding the other predictors constant.

Standardizing around the overall sample mean is a form of **grand-mean
centering**. As Session 2 notes, this fixes the reference point of every
predictor at its overall average, so the intercept $\gamma_{00}$ is the
expected job satisfaction of a teacher at the average level of all
predictors -- which is how it is interpreted throughout this report.
Model fit is unaffected by centering; only the interpretation of the
intercept changes. The alternative, group-mean centering, would instead
express each teacher relative to their own school's mean and would allow
the within-school and between-school components of a Level-1 predictor
to be estimated separately (by additionally entering the school means as
Level-2 predictors). That decomposition is not pursued here: the
research question concerns the association of each characteristic with
the outcome overall rather than a contrast between its within- and
between-school components, and adding five school means would exceed the
predictor budget the assignment allows. It is noted in the limitations
as a possible extension.


## Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection

Following the course's taught modeling strategy (Session 3, "Modeling
strategy" and "Testing Strategy: Summary"): after testing which random
effects are necessary (done above), the fixed effects are tested using
ML, removing non-significant interactions first (there are none in
this model) and then non-significant main effects. This is implemented
below as iterative backward elimination: at each step, the single
least-significant fixed effect (largest nested-LRT p-value against the
current model) is dropped if its p-value exceeds .05, the model is
refit, and the remaining terms are re-tested. This repeats until every
remaining fixed effect is significant, which correctly handles cases
where dropping one predictor changes another predictor's significance
(relevant here, given the age/experience correlation reported above).

```{r,results='markup'}

alpha <- .05

candidate_terms <- c(
  "age_z", "experience_z", "working_hours_z", "ict_use_z",
  "stress_z", "lack_of_respect_z", "ses_disadvantage_z"
)

# Random-effects structure already established above (final_re_formula)
# -- held FIXED while fixed effects are tested below.
fit_step_model <- function(terms) {
  f <- as.formula(
    paste0(
      "satisfaction ~ ",
      paste(terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + ", final_re_formula
    )
  )
  lmer(f, data = data_model_clean, REML = FALSE)
}

current_terms   <- candidate_terms
step_num        <- 1
elimination_log <- data.frame()

repeat {

  current_step_model <- fit_step_model(current_terms)

  term_pvals <- sapply(current_terms, function(term) {
    reduced_terms <- setdiff(current_terms, term)
    reduced_model <- fit_step_model(reduced_terms)
    test          <- anova(reduced_model, current_step_model)
    test$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
  })

  cat("\n--- Step", step_num, "-- current terms:",
      paste(current_terms, collapse = ", "), "---\n")
  print(round(term_pvals, 4))

  worst_term <- names(which.max(term_pvals))
  worst_p    <- max(term_pvals)

  elimination_log <- rbind(
    elimination_log,
    data.frame(
      step = step_num,
      least_significant_term = worst_term,
      p_value = round(worst_p, 4),
      action = ifelse(worst_p > alpha, "dropped",
                       "stop -- all remaining terms significant")
    )
  )

  if (worst_p <= alpha) {
    cat("\nAll remaining fixed effects significant at alpha =", alpha,
        "-- stopping.\n")
    break
  }

  cat("Dropping:", worst_term, "(p =", round(worst_p, 4), ")\n")
  current_terms <- setdiff(current_terms, worst_term)

  if (length(current_terms) == 0) {
    cat("All fixed effects eliminated -- stopping.\n")
    break
  }

  step_num <- step_num + 1
}

cat("\n===================== Elimination log =====================\n")
print(elimination_log, row.names = FALSE)

# retained_terms is used everywhere below (Final Model and the
# Logistic Extension) so both analyses always match this decision --
# never hardcode the predictor list again after this point.
retained_terms <- current_terms
dropped_terms  <- setdiff(candidate_terms, retained_terms)

cat("\nRetained fixed effects:", paste(retained_terms, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Dropped fixed effects:",   paste(dropped_terms,  collapse = ", "), "\n")

```

Terms are dropped one at a time, starting from the term with the
largest nested-LRT p-value at each step, and the remaining terms are
re-tested after each removal -- this is what makes the procedure
genuinely stepwise rather than a single-pass drop of everything
non-significant in the saturated model at once. `r if (length(dropped_terms) > 0) paste0("Based on this procedure, ", paste(dropped_terms, collapse = " and "), if (length(dropped_terms) > 1) " were" else " was", " dropped from the fixed-effects specification; ", paste(retained_terms, collapse = ", "), " were retained.") else "Based on this procedure, all seven predictors remained significant and none were dropped."`


## Final Model


```{r,results='markup'}
# Correlations between predictors
dat7 <- data_model_clean[, c(
  "age_z",
  "experience_z",
  "working_hours_z",
  "ict_use_z",
  "stress_z",
  "lack_of_respect_z",
  "ses_disadvantage_z"
)]

round(cor(dat7, use = "complete.obs"), 1)

```

Multicollinearity was assessed by examining the correlations among the predictor variables. Most predictors showed only weak correlations with each other. However, age and teaching experience were strongly positively correlated (r=.90), indicating substantial overlap between these two predictors. The remaining correlations were relatively small, with the largest additional correlation being between lack of respect and the proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged students (r=.40). Thus, particular caution is warranted when interpreting the separate effects of age and teaching experience.

Two points are worth noting in light of the backward-elimination procedure reported above. First, both age and teaching experience were retained by that procedure, and both remained statistically significant with coefficients of opposite sign despite their high correlation. Severe multicollinearity typically inflates standard errors enough to render one or both such predictors non-significant, which did not occur here; the correlation is therefore best treated as a caution for interpretation rather than as evidence of an unstable model. Second, because $r=.90$ corresponds to a variance inflation factor of roughly $1/(1-.90^2)\approx5.3$ for these two terms, their standard errors are approximately $\sqrt{5.3}\approx2.3$ times larger than they would be if the two predictors were uncorrelated. Their individual coefficients should accordingly be read as the effect of each variable *holding the other constant* -- a comparison between teachers of the same age but differing experience, and vice versa -- rather than as the total effect of ageing or of accumulating experience.


```{r,results='markup'}

# The fixed-effects part of the formula (retained_terms) comes from
# the Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection section above; the random-
# effects part (final_re_formula) was decided programmatically
# earlier, based on whether the ICT random slope survives on top of
# the stress random slope. This guarantees the fitted model always
# matches both decisions -- never hardcode the predictor list here.
final_model <- lmer(
  as.formula(
    paste0(
      "satisfaction ~ ",
      paste(retained_terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + ", final_re_formula
    )
  ),
  data = data_model_clean,
  REML = TRUE
)

summary(final_model)
VarCorr(final_model)
isSingular(final_model)

# Small helpers so every b/p reported below is read directly
# from final_model rather than typed in by hand, so the text
# automatically stays correct however the ICT-slope decision and
# the fixed-effects elimination above turn out. If a term was
# dropped during elimination, these return a placeholder instead
# of erroring, so the document still knits -- the surrounding prose
# in "Explaining Fixed Effects" below still needs a manual pass once
# you know which terms were actually dropped (see the note there).
fixef_b <- function(term) {
  if (!(term %in% retained_terms)) return(NA_real_)
  round(summary(final_model)$coefficients[term, "Estimate"], 3)
}
fixef_p <- function(term) {
  if (!(term %in% retained_terms)) return("[dropped from final model]")
  p <- summary(final_model)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|t|)"]
  if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste0("= ", signif(p, 2))
}
term_retained <- function(term) term %in% retained_terms


```


### Explaining Fixed Effects

Because the predictors were standardized, the fixed-effect coefficients
represent the expected change in teacher job satisfaction associated
with a one-standard-deviation increase in the corresponding predictor,
holding all other predictors constant. All five coefficients reported
below are statistically significant, since the backward-elimination
procedure retained only predictors that improved model fit; the two
predictors removed during that procedure (weekly working hours and the
proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged students) are discussed
at the end of this section.

Perceived stress showed the strongest association with teacher job
satisfaction. The fixed effect of stress was negative and statistically
significant ($b=`r fixef_b("stress_z")`$, $p `r fixef_p("stress_z")`$).
Thus, a one-standard-deviation increase in perceived stress was
associated with an average decrease of approximately
$`r abs(fixef_b("stress_z"))`$ points in teacher job satisfaction,
holding the other predictors constant. `r ifelse(ict_slope_retained, "Because stress and ICT use both have random slopes in this model, this coefficient represents the average (fixed) effect of stress across schools, while the corresponding random-slope variance (reported below) captures how much that effect differs from school to school.", "")`

Age was also negatively associated with job satisfaction
($b=`r fixef_b("age_z")`$, $p `r fixef_p("age_z")`$). A
one-standard-deviation increase in age was associated with an average
decrease of approximately $`r abs(fixef_b("age_z"))`$ points in job
satisfaction, controlling for the other predictors.

Teaching experience was positively associated with job satisfaction
($b=`r fixef_b("experience_z")`$, $p `r fixef_p("experience_z")`$).
Thus, a one-standard-deviation increase in teaching experience was
associated with an average increase of approximately
$`r fixef_b("experience_z")`$ points in job satisfaction, holding the
remaining predictors constant.

ICT use was positively associated with job satisfaction
($b=`r fixef_b("ict_use_z")`$, $p `r fixef_p("ict_use_z")`$). A
one-standard-deviation increase in ICT use was associated with an
average increase of approximately $`r fixef_b("ict_use_z")`$ points in
job satisfaction. `r ifelse(ict_slope_retained, "Unlike the other teacher-level predictors, ICT use also has a random slope in this model: the value above is the average effect across schools, and the estimated slope variance (below) shows that this association is not the same size in every school.", "As established above, ICT use's random slope did not survive as a stable addition once the stress random slope was already in the model, so it is modeled here with a fixed (average) effect only.")`

At the school level, lack of respect for teachers was negatively
associated with teacher job satisfaction
($b=`r fixef_b("lack_of_respect_z")`$, $p `r fixef_p("lack_of_respect_z")`$).
Thus, a one-standard-deviation increase in the school-level measure of
lack of respect was associated with an average decrease of approximately
$`r abs(fixef_b("lack_of_respect_z"))`$ points in teacher job
satisfaction, holding the other predictors constant.

**Predictors removed during model selection.** Two predictors did not
survive the backward-elimination procedure and are therefore not part
of the final model. The proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged
students was removed first ($p=.511$ in the saturated model), and
weekly working hours was removed at the second step ($p=.149$ in the
model that no longer contained the SES term). In both cases, removing
the predictor did not produce a significant deterioration in model fit,
indicating that neither variable contributed detectably to explaining
variation in teacher job satisfaction once the other predictors were
accounted for. Following the interpretive convention used throughout
this report, this is evidence of *insufficient support* for an
association, not positive evidence that the true effect is exactly
zero.


### Overall Interpretation

Overall, the final model indicates that four teacher-level
characteristics are significantly associated with teacher job
satisfaction. Perceived stress showed the strongest negative
association, followed by age, whereas teaching experience and ICT use
showed positive associations with job satisfaction. Weekly working
hours did not survive model selection.

At the school level, lack of respect for teachers was significantly and
negatively associated with job satisfaction and was retained, whereas
the proportion of socioeconomically disadvantaged students was removed
during backward elimination.

In addition to these fixed effects, the non-zero random-slope variance
for perceived stress indicates that the relationship between stress and
job satisfaction varies across schools. Thus, the negative association
between perceived stress and job satisfaction represents an average
effect across schools, while the magnitude of this association differs
between schools. `r ifelse(ict_slope_retained, "The same is true for ICT use: its random-slope variance indicates that the (positive, on average) association between ICT use and job satisfaction also differs from school to school, rather than being fixed at the same size everywhere.", "ICT use, by contrast, is retained only as a fixed effect, since its random slope did not hold up once the stress random slope was already in the model (see the model-selection resolution above): its association with satisfaction is treated as constant in size across schools.")`



### Explained Variance

A multilevel model can be summarised by how much of the variance at each
level it accounts for. Following Session 3 ("Explained variance"), a
pseudo $R^2$ is computed separately for the Level-1 residual variance
and the Level-2 random-intercept variance, by comparing variance
components across three nested random-intercept models: an empty
baseline model, a model adding the retained Level-1 predictors, and a
model adding the retained Level-2 predictor. Random-intercept models are
used throughout so that a single $\sigma^2_{u0}$ is comparable across
the three fits; the random slopes of the final model would split the
Level-2 variance into several components and make the comparison
ambiguous.

$$
R^2_{11}=\frac{\sigma^2_{\epsilon|b}-\sigma^2_{\epsilon|m1}}{\sigma^2_{\epsilon|b}},
\qquad
R^2_{21}=\frac{\sigma^2_{u|b}-\sigma^2_{u|m1}}{\sigma^2_{u|b}}
$$

$$
R^2_{12}=\frac{\sigma^2_{\epsilon|m1}-\sigma^2_{\epsilon|m2}}{\sigma^2_{\epsilon|m1}},
\qquad
R^2_{22}=\frac{\sigma^2_{u|m1}-\sigma^2_{u|m2}}{\sigma^2_{u|m1}}
$$

```{r explained_variance, results='markup'}

# ============================================================
# EXPLAINED VARIANCE (PSEUDO R-SQUARED)
# ============================================================
# Session 3, "Explained variance": compare the variance
# components of three nested RANDOM-INTERCEPT models.
#   b  = baseline (empty) model
#   m1 = + Level-1 predictors
#   m2 = + Level-2 predictors
# REML is used, since these are variance-component estimates
# rather than nested likelihood-ratio tests.

l1_retained <- intersect(
  retained_terms,
  c("age_z", "experience_z", "working_hours_z", "ict_use_z", "stress_z")
)
l2_retained <- intersect(
  retained_terms,
  c("lack_of_respect_z", "ses_disadvantage_z")
)

m_var_base <- lmer(
  satisfaction ~ 1 + (1 | school_id),
  data = data_model_clean, REML = TRUE
)

m_var_l1 <- lmer(
  as.formula(paste0(
    "satisfaction ~ ", paste(l1_retained, collapse = " + "),
    " + (1 | school_id)"
  )),
  data = data_model_clean, REML = TRUE
)

m_var_l2 <- lmer(
  as.formula(paste0(
    "satisfaction ~ ",
    paste(c(l1_retained, l2_retained), collapse = " + "),
    " + (1 | school_id)"
  )),
  data = data_model_clean, REML = TRUE
)

get_vc <- function(m) {
  v <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m))
  c(
    u0  = v$vcov[v$grp == "school_id" & !is.na(v$var1) & v$var1 == "(Intercept)"],
    eps = v$vcov[v$grp == "Residual"]
  )
}

vc_b  <- get_vc(m_var_base)
vc_m1 <- get_vc(m_var_l1)
vc_m2 <- get_vc(m_var_l2)

variance_table <- data.frame(
  model = c("Baseline (empty)", "+ Level-1 predictors", "+ Level-2 predictor"),
  sigma2_eps = round(c(vc_b["eps"], vc_m1["eps"], vc_m2["eps"]), 5),
  sigma2_u0  = round(c(vc_b["u0"],  vc_m1["u0"],  vc_m2["u0"]),  5)
)
print(variance_table, row.names = FALSE)

R2_11 <- (vc_b["eps"]  - vc_m1["eps"]) / vc_b["eps"]    # L1 var explained by L1 preds
R2_21 <- (vc_b["u0"]   - vc_m1["u0"])  / vc_b["u0"]     # L2 var explained by L1 preds
R2_12 <- (vc_m1["eps"] - vc_m2["eps"]) / vc_m1["eps"]   # L1 var explained by L2 pred
R2_22 <- (vc_m1["u0"]  - vc_m2["u0"])  / vc_m1["u0"]    # L2 var explained by L2 pred

r2_table <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("R2_11 (L1 var, L1 predictors)",
               "R2_21 (L2 var, L1 predictors)",
               "R2_12 (L1 var, L2 predictor)",
               "R2_22 (L2 var, L2 predictor)"),
  value    = round(c(R2_11, R2_21, R2_12, R2_22), 4),
  percent  = paste0(round(100 * c(R2_11, R2_21, R2_12, R2_22), 2), "%")
)
print(r2_table, row.names = FALSE)

```

Note that $R^2_{21}$ can in principle come out negative. As the lecture
notes, adding Level-1 predictors can *increase* the estimated Level-2
variance when schools differ substantively in the distribution of those
predictors, because the random intercept then has to absorb composition
differences between schools that the raw baseline model had folded into
the residual. A negative value is therefore a substantive result rather
than a computational error, and is reported as such.

**Results.** The Level-1 residual variance falls from 3.508 in the empty
model to 2.617 once the four teacher-level predictors are added, so
$R^2_{11}=.254$: the teacher-level characteristics account for about
25.4% of the variance in job satisfaction *between teachers within the
same school*. The same predictors also reduce the school-level variance,
from 0.0375 to 0.0341, giving $R^2_{21}=.091$. This second figure is not
a school-level effect in its own right: it reflects the fact that
schools differ in the composition of their teaching staff, so part of
what looked like between-school variance in the empty model was actually
a difference in who works where.

Adding the school-level predictor then produces the pattern the
multilevel framework predicts. It explains none of the Level-1 variance
($R^2_{12}=.000$; the residual variance moves only from 2.61667 to
2.61664), which is exactly right -- lack of respect is constant within a
school, so it cannot possibly account for why two teachers *in the same
school* differ. What it does explain is between-school variance: the
school-level variance falls further from 0.0341 to 0.0294, so
$R^2_{22}=.138$, meaning the single school-level predictor accounts for
roughly 13.8% of the between-school differences that remained after
controlling for staff composition.

These figures should be read against the ICC of 1.06%. Because so little
of the total variance in job satisfaction lies between schools in the
first place, explaining 13.8% of that small share is a modest
contribution in absolute terms. The substantial explanatory work in this
model is done at Level 1, which is consistent with the fixed-effects
results, where the teacher-level predictors -- and stress in particular
-- carry far larger coefficients than the school-level one.


### Level 1: Teacher Level

$$
satisfaction_{ij}
=
\beta_{0j}
+
\gamma_{10}\text{age\_z}_{ij}
+
\gamma_{20}\text{experience\_z}_{ij}
+
`r if (ict_slope_retained) "\\beta_{4j}\\text{ict\\_use\\_z}_{ij}" else "\\gamma_{40}\\text{ict\\_use\\_z}_{ij}"`
+
\beta_{5j}\text{stress\_z}_{ij}
+
\varepsilon_{ij}
$$

### Level 2: School Level

$$
\beta_{0j}
=
\gamma_{00}
+
\gamma_{01}\text{lack\_of\_respect\_z}_j
+
u_{0j}
$$

`r if (ict_slope_retained) "$$\n\\beta_{4j}\n=\n\\gamma_{40}\n+\nu_{4j}\n$$" else ""`

$$
\beta_{5j}
=
\gamma_{50}
+
u_{5j}
$$

For the uncorrelated random-slope model,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(u_{0j},u_{5j})=0`r if (ict_slope_retained) ",\\ \\operatorname{Cov}(u_{0j},u_{4j})=0,\\ \\operatorname{Cov}(u_{4j},u_{5j})=0" else ""`.
$$

### Final Combined Model (with Random Slope)

$$
\begin{aligned}
satisfaction_{ij}
={}&
\gamma_{00}
+
\gamma_{10}\text{age\_z}_{ij}
+
\gamma_{20}\text{experience\_z}_{ij}
+
\gamma_{40}\text{ict\_use\_z}_{ij}
\\
&+
\gamma_{50}\text{stress\_z}_{ij}
+
\gamma_{01}\text{lack\_of\_respect\_z}_j
\\
&+
u_{0j}
`r if (ict_slope_retained) "+\nu_{4j}\\text{ict\\_use\\_z}_{ij}" else ""`
+
u_{5j}\text{stress\_z}_{ij}
+
\varepsilon_{ij}.
\end{aligned}
$$

`r if (ict_slope_retained) "Here $\\beta_{4j} = \\gamma_{40} + u_{4j}$ replaces the earlier fixed-only $\\gamma_{40}\\text{ict\\_use\\_z}_{ij}$ term, since the ICT random slope is retained in the final model." else ""`

To extend the main analysis to a non-continuous outcome, a multilevel logistic regression model was estimated to examine teachers' intentions to leave the teaching profession. The binary dependent variable, `leave`, indicates whether a teacher has considered leaving the teaching profession. A value of 1 indicates that the teacher has considered leaving, whereas a value of 0 indicates that the teacher has not.

The same teacher-level and school-level predictors retained by the main analysis's Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection (`retained_terms`) are used here as well, rather than re-deriving a separate predictor set for this outcome -- see the note above the Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection code for why. `r paste0("The retained predictors are: ", paste(retained_terms, collapse = ", "), ".")` Because teachers are nested within schools, a random intercept for school was included.

A logistic rather than a linear mixed model was used because the dependent variable is binary. Following the estimation procedures discussed in the lecture, the model assumes a Bernoulli distribution for the outcome and uses the logit link. The model was estimated by maximum likelihood using numerical approximation. In `glmer()`, the default estimation uses the Laplace approximation. The lecture notes emphasize that ML, rather than REML, is used for GLMMs and for likelihood-based model comparisons.

```{r logistic_model, results='markup'}

# ============================================================
# EXTENSION ANALYSIS
# Multilevel Logistic Regression
# Outcome: Intention to Leave
# ============================================================

# Binary outcome:
# leave = 1: seriously considered leaving classroom teaching
# leave = 0: did not seriously consider leaving classroom teaching


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Check the binary outcome
# ------------------------------------------------------------

table(
  data_model_clean$leave,
  useNA = "ifany"
)

round(
  100 * prop.table(
    table(data_model_clean$leave)
  ),
  2
)


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Create the analysis dataset
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Only the outcome, school_id, and the predictors actually
# RETAINED by the main analysis's backward elimination
# (retained_terms) are selected here -- consistent with the rule
# stated above ("never hardcode the predictor list again after
# this point"). working_hours_z and ses_disadvantage_z were
# dropped from the fixed-effects model and are never used in
# model_logistic, so they must not be part of the complete-case
# filter either: including them here would let a teacher with
# missing working_hours_z or ses_disadvantage_z be excluded from
# the logistic analysis even though those two variables never
# appear in any logistic model.

data_logistic <- data_model_clean %>%
  dplyr::select(
    leave,
    dplyr::all_of(retained_terms),
    school_id
  ) %>%
  na.omit()

# Number of teachers
nrow(data_logistic)

# Number of schools
length(
  unique(data_logistic$school_id)
)


# ============================================================
# 3. NULL MODEL: RANDOM INTERCEPT ONLY
# ============================================================
# The null model contains only a random intercept for school.
#
# It allows the baseline log-odds of considering leaving
# the teaching profession to vary across schools.

model_logistic_null <- glmer(
  leave ~
    (1 | school_id),
  data = data_logistic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 1
)

summary(model_logistic_null)


# ============================================================
# 4. FULL RANDOM-INTERCEPT MODEL
# ============================================================
# The model contains the SAME predictors retained by the main
# continuous-outcome analysis's Stepwise Fixed-Effects Selection
# (retained_terms), not a hardcoded list and not an independently
# re-derived set. Keeping the same predictor set across both
# outcomes is intentional: an "extension" analysis is meant to
# test whether the SAME teacher- and school-level characteristics
# matter for a different (here: binary) outcome, not to re-derive
# a new predictor set from scratch. This also satisfies the
# syllabus requirement that both DVs use the same predictor set.
#
# Random intercept:
# (1 | school_id)

model_logistic <- glmer(
  as.formula(
    paste0(
      "leave ~ ",
      paste(retained_terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + (1 | school_id)"
    )
  ),
  data = data_logistic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ = 1
)

summary(model_logistic)


# ============================================================
# 5. FIXED-EFFECT MODEL COMPARISON
# ============================================================
# Compare the full random-intercept model with the
# random-intercept-only null model.
#
# H0:
# All retained fixed-effect coefficients are equal to zero.
#
# HA:
# At least one fixed-effect coefficient is different from zero.

fixed_effect_LRT <- anova(
  model_logistic_null,
  model_logistic,
  test = "Chisq"
)

fixed_effect_LRT


# ============================================================
# 6. RANDOM-SLOPE TESTS FOR ALL TEACHER-LEVEL PREDICTORS
# ============================================================
# This mirrors the Random Slope Test of the main (continuous)
# analysis: every teacher-level predictor in the retained set is
# given its own uncorrelated random slope, tested against the
# random-intercept-only model by LRT, with the same p/2 boundary
# correction (the slope variance sits on the boundary sigma^2 >= 0
# under H0) and the same stability requirement (non-singular +
# clean convergence).
#
# Only Level-1 (teacher-level) predictors can have random slopes
# across schools; lack_of_respect_z is a Level-2 (school-level)
# variable and is constant within a school, so it is excluded.

l1_terms <- intersect(
  retained_terms,
  c("age_z", "experience_z", "working_hours_z", "ict_use_z", "stress_z")
)

converged_glmm <- function(model) {
  conv    <- model@optinfo$conv
  opt_ok  <- is.null(conv$opt) || conv$opt == 0
  lme4_ok <- is.null(conv$lme4$code)
  opt_ok && lme4_ok
}

rs_results <- data.frame()
rs_models  <- list()

for (v in l1_terms) {

  form_v <- as.formula(
    paste0(
      "leave ~ ",
      paste(retained_terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + (1 | school_id) + (-1 + ", v, " | school_id)"
    )
  )

  mod_v <- try(
    glmer(
      form_v,
      data   = data_logistic,
      family = binomial(link = "logit"),
      nAGQ   = 1
    ),
    silent = TRUE
  )

  if (inherits(mod_v, "try-error")) {
    rs_results <- rbind(rs_results, data.frame(
      predictor = v, chisq = NA, p_raw = NA, p_corrected = NA,
      singular = NA, converged = FALSE, decision = "model failed to fit"
    ))
    next
  }

  rs_models[[v]] <- mod_v

  test_v <- anova(model_logistic, mod_v, test = "Chisq")
  chisq_v <- test_v$Chisq[2]
  p_raw_v <- test_v$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
  p_cor_v <- 0.5 * p_raw_v          # boundary correction, as in the main analysis

  sing_v  <- isSingular(mod_v)
  conv_v  <- converged_glmm(mod_v)
  keep_v  <- !is.na(p_cor_v) && p_cor_v < .05 && !sing_v && conv_v

  rs_results <- rbind(rs_results, data.frame(
    predictor   = v,
    chisq       = round(chisq_v, 3),
    p_raw       = signif(p_raw_v, 3),
    p_corrected = signif(p_cor_v, 3),
    singular    = sing_v,
    converged   = conv_v,
    decision    = ifelse(keep_v, "RETAIN random slope", "do not retain")
  ))

  cat("\n=== Random slope (logistic):", v, "===\n")
  print(test_v)
  cat("Boundary-corrected p:", p_cor_v,
      " | singular:", sing_v, " | converged:", conv_v, "\n")
}

cat("\n============ Random-slope test summary (logistic) ============\n")
print(rs_results, row.names = FALSE)

slopes_retained <- rs_results$predictor[
  rs_results$decision == "RETAIN random slope"
]

cat("\nRandom slopes retained (logistic):",
    if (length(slopes_retained)) paste(slopes_retained, collapse = ", ") else "none",
    "\n")


# ============================================================
# 7. COVARIANCE TESTS FOR THE RETAINED RANDOM SLOPES
# ============================================================
# For every slope retained in step 6, test whether it should be
# allowed to correlate with the random intercept -- the same H8
# test used in the main analysis. No boundary correction is
# needed here: a covariance is not a boundary parameter.

cov_results <- data.frame()

for (v in slopes_retained) {

  form_corr <- as.formula(
    paste0(
      "leave ~ ",
      paste(retained_terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + (1 + ", v, " | school_id)"
    )
  )

  mod_corr <- try(
    glmer(
      form_corr,
      data   = data_logistic,
      family = binomial(link = "logit"),
      nAGQ   = 1
    ),
    silent = TRUE
  )

  if (inherits(mod_corr, "try-error")) {
    cov_results <- rbind(cov_results, data.frame(
      predictor = v, chisq = NA, p = NA,
      singular = NA, converged = FALSE,
      decision = "correlated model failed to fit -- keep uncorrelated"
    ))
    next
  }

  test_c  <- anova(rs_models[[v]], mod_corr, test = "Chisq")
  chisq_c <- test_c$Chisq[2]
  p_c     <- test_c$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
  sing_c  <- isSingular(mod_corr)
  conv_c  <- converged_glmm(mod_corr)
  keep_c  <- !is.na(p_c) && p_c < .05 && !sing_c && conv_c

  cov_results <- rbind(cov_results, data.frame(
    predictor = v,
    chisq     = round(chisq_c, 3),
    p         = signif(p_c, 3),
    singular  = sing_c,
    converged = conv_c,
    decision  = ifelse(keep_c,
                       "use CORRELATED specification",
                       "keep uncorrelated specification")
  ))

  cat("\n=== Covariance test (logistic):", v, "===\n")
  print(test_c)
  cat("singular:", sing_c, " | converged:", conv_c, "\n")
}

if (nrow(cov_results)) {
  cat("\n============ Covariance test summary (logistic) ============\n")
  print(cov_results, row.names = FALSE)
} else {
  cat("\nNo random slopes retained, so no covariance test is required.\n")
}


# ============================================================
# 8. RANDOM-EFFECTS STRUCTURE OF THE LOGISTIC MODEL
# ============================================================
# Built programmatically from steps 6-7 so the fitted model always
# matches the test results rather than being hardcoded.

if (length(slopes_retained) == 0) {
  logistic_re_formula <- "(1 | school_id)"
} else {
  logistic_re_formula <- paste0(
    "(1 + ", paste(slopes_retained, collapse = " + "), " || school_id)"
  )
}

cat("\nLogistic random-effects structure:", logistic_re_formula, "\n")


# ============================================================
# 9. FINAL LOGISTIC MODEL
# ============================================================
# The fixed-effects part is INHERITED from the main analysis
# (retained_terms) and is not re-selected here. Session 6's own
# worked example follows the same pattern: in the toenail models
# the fixed effects (treatment + month + treatment:month) are
# identical in mod1, mod2 and mod3, and every model comparison
# concerns the random-effects structure only. Model selection for
# a binary outcome is therefore carried out in steps 6-8 above;
# the fixed effects are TESTED (joint LRT in step 5, individual
# Wald z-tests below) but are not used as a selection criterion.

model_logistic_final <- glmer(
  as.formula(
    paste0(
      "leave ~ ",
      paste(retained_terms, collapse = " + "),
      " + ", logistic_re_formula
    )
  ),
  data   = data_logistic,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  nAGQ   = 1
)

final_model_choice <- paste0(
  "shared predictor set + random-effects structure ",
  logistic_re_formula
)

cat("Selected final logistic model:", final_model_choice, "\n")

summary(model_logistic_final)
isSingular(model_logistic_final)
model_logistic_final@optinfo$conv


# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 9.1 Documentation only: which predictors would a backward
#     elimination on THIS outcome have removed?
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Reported as a one-line note in the write-up, not as a competing
# model. The predictor set is deliberately held identical across
# the two dependent variables so that each predictor's role can
# be compared between outcomes; re-selecting here would make that
# comparison impossible and would breach the requirement that
# both DVs use the same predictors.

wald_p <- summary(model_logistic_final)$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
wald_p <- wald_p[names(wald_p) != "(Intercept)"]

ns_for_leave <- names(wald_p)[wald_p >= .05]

cat("\nNon-significant for intention to leave (retained anyway):",
    if (length(ns_for_leave)) paste(ns_for_leave, collapse = ", ") else "none",
    "\n")


# ============================================================
# 10. MODEL FIT COMPARISON
# ============================================================
# Candidates: the null model, the shared-predictor random-intercept
# model, every single-slope model fitted in step 6, and the final
# model selected in step 9.

fit_candidates <- c(
  list(
    null    = model_logistic_null,
    shared  = model_logistic,
    final   = model_logistic_final
  ),
  setNames(rs_models, paste0("rs_", names(rs_models)))
)

fit_table <- data.frame(
  model = names(fit_candidates),
  npar  = sapply(fit_candidates, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC   = round(sapply(fit_candidates, AIC), 3),
  BIC   = round(sapply(fit_candidates, BIC), 3)
)

print(fit_table, row.names = FALSE)


# ============================================================
# 11. FIXED EFFECTS OF THE FINAL MODEL
# ============================================================
# Coefficients are estimated on the log-odds scale.

summary(
  model_logistic_final
)$coefficients


# ============================================================
# 12. ODDS RATIOS
# ============================================================
# Exponentiating a logistic regression coefficient
# gives the corresponding odds ratio.

odds_ratios <- exp(
  fixef(model_logistic_final)
)

odds_ratios

# Compact results table
logistic_results <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(
    fixef(model_logistic_final)
  ),

  Estimate = fixef(
    model_logistic_final
  ),

  Odds_Ratio = exp(
    fixef(model_logistic_final)
  ),

  SE = summary(
    model_logistic_final
  )$coefficients[, "Std. Error"],

  z = summary(
    model_logistic_final
  )$coefficients[, "z value"],

  p = summary(
    model_logistic_final
  )$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

logistic_results


# ============================================================
# 13. 95% CONFIDENCE INTERVALS FOR ODDS RATIOS
# ============================================================

beta <- fixef(
  model_logistic_final
)

se <- sqrt(
  diag(
    vcov(model_logistic_final)
  )
)

OR_results <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(beta),

  Estimate = beta,

  Odds_Ratio = exp(beta),

  CI_lower = exp(
    beta - 1.96 * se
  ),

  CI_upper = exp(
    beta + 1.96 * se
  ),

  SE = se,

  z = beta / se,

  p = summary(
    model_logistic_final
  )$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
)

OR_results


# ============================================================
# 14. RANDOM EFFECTS
# ============================================================

VarCorr(
  model_logistic_final
)

# School-level random-intercept variance
school_variance <- as.numeric(
  VarCorr(
    model_logistic_final
  )$school_id[1]
)

school_variance

# School-level random-intercept SD
school_sd <- sqrt(
  school_variance
)

school_sd


# ============================================================
# 15. RANDOM SLOPE VARIANCES
# ============================================================
# This is relevant if the final model contains a
# random stress slope.

if (
  "stress_z" %in%
  rownames(
    as.data.frame(
      VarCorr(model_logistic_final)$school_id
    )
  )
) {

  stress_slope_variance <- as.numeric(
    VarCorr(
      model_logistic_final
    )$school_id["stress_z", "stress_z"]
  )

  stress_slope_sd <- sqrt(
    stress_slope_variance
  )

  stress_slope_variance

  stress_slope_sd
}


# ============================================================
# 16. INTRACLASS CORRELATION COEFFICIENT
# ============================================================
# Two ICCs are reported here, for the same reason the continuous-
# outcome ICC (Session 2-5, mod0) was computed from the EMPTY model
# before any predictors were added: the "standard" ICC that describes
# how strongly teachers cluster within schools BY DESIGN -- independent
# of which predictors are later chosen -- is the UNCONDITIONAL one,
# taken from model_logistic_null. That is the figure comparable to the
# 1.06% reported for job satisfaction.
#
# The CONDITIONAL ICC below (using school_variance, i.e. AFTER the 5
# retained predictors are already in the model) is also informative --
# it shows how much between-school heterogeneity is left over once the
# predictors are accounted for -- but it is a different quantity, and
# is reported and labeled as such rather than as a substitute for the
# unconditional ICC.
#
# For a random-intercept logistic model, the Level-1
# residual variance on the latent scale is fixed at:
#
# pi^2 / 3
#
# (this is a property of the standard logistic distribution,
# not something estimated from the data)

# --- Unconditional ICC: null model, before any predictors ---
null_variance_logistic <- as.numeric(
  VarCorr(model_logistic_null)$school_id[1]
)

icc_logistic_unconditional <- null_variance_logistic /
  (
    null_variance_logistic +
      pi^2 / 3
  )

icc_logistic_unconditional

100 * icc_logistic_unconditional

# --- Conditional ICC: final model, after the 5 predictors ---
icc_logistic_conditional <- school_variance /
  (
    school_variance +
      pi^2 / 3
  )

icc_logistic_conditional

100 * icc_logistic_conditional

# kept for compatibility with the results table below
icc_logistic <- icc_logistic_conditional


# ============================================================
# 17. MODEL DIAGNOSTICS
# ============================================================

# Singularity
isSingular(
  model_logistic_final
)

# Convergence
model_logistic_final@optinfo$conv


# ============================================================
# 18. PREDICTED PROBABILITIES
# ============================================================
# Conditional predictions include school-specific
# random effects.

data_logistic$predicted_probability <-
  predict(
    model_logistic_final,
    type = "response"
  )

# Predicted probability curve as a function of perceived stress
# (the strongest predictor), following the same approach used in
# Session 6, Part 2.3 for the simple logistic regression example:
# the model's fitted probabilities are plotted against the predictor,
# together with the fitted probability curve implied by the fixed
# effects (other predictors held at their mean = 0, since all are
# standardized; school random intercept held at u0 = 0, i.e. an
# average school).

b_log_final <- fixef(model_logistic_final)

yhat_stress <- function(x) {
  plogis(b_log_final[["(Intercept)"]] + b_log_final[["stress_z"]] * x)
}

plot(
  data_logistic$stress_z,
  data_logistic$predicted_probability,
  xlab = "Perceived stress (standardized)",
  ylab = "P(considering leaving)",
  main = "Predicted probability of leaving vs. stress",
  pch = 16,
  col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.15),
  ylim = c(0, 1)
)
curve(
  yhat_stress,
  from = min(data_logistic$stress_z),
  to   = max(data_logistic$stress_z),
  add  = TRUE,
  col  = "red",
  lwd  = 2
)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 3)


# ============================================================
# 19. FINAL COMPACT RESULTS TABLE
# ============================================================

final_logistic_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(
    fixef(model_logistic_final)
  ),

  Estimate = round(
    fixef(model_logistic_final),
    3
  ),

  Odds_Ratio = round(
    exp(fixef(model_logistic_final)),
    3
  ),

  SE = round(
    summary(
      model_logistic_final
    )$coefficients[, "Std. Error"],
    3
  ),

  z = round(
    summary(
      model_logistic_final
    )$coefficients[, "z value"],
    3
  ),

  p = round(
    summary(
      model_logistic_final
    )$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"],
    4
  ),

  ICC_unconditional_percent = round(
    100 * icc_logistic_unconditional,
    2
  ),

  ICC_conditional_percent = round(
    100 * icc_logistic_conditional,
    2
  )
)

final_logistic_table


```


## Extension Analysis: Multilevel Logistic Regression

To extend the main analysis to a non-continuous outcome, a multilevel logistic regression model was estimated to examine teachers' intentions to leave the teaching profession. The binary outcome indicated whether a teacher had seriously considered leaving classroom teaching. A value of 1 indicated that the teacher had seriously considered leaving, whereas a value of 0 indicated that the teacher had not. The coding of the outcome was based on the original questionnaire response, with responses recoded as 1 = yes and 0 = no.

The final estimation sample consisted of 2,599 teachers nested within 192 schools. Of these teachers, 559 (21.51%) had seriously considered leaving the teaching profession, while 2,040 (78.49%) had not.

Because the dependent variable was binary, a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Bernoulli distribution and a logit link was estimated. The model included the same predictors retained by the main analysis's backward-elimination procedure -- four teacher-level predictors (age, teaching experience, ICT use, and perceived stress) and one school-level predictor (lack of respect for teachers). Weekly working hours and socio-economic disadvantage were not part of that retained set and are therefore absent from this model as well. A random intercept for school was included to account for the nesting of teachers within schools.

Following the estimation procedure discussed in the lecture, the model was estimated using maximum likelihood with the Laplace approximation (`glmer()`, `nAGQ = 1`). Unlike the linear mixed model, REML was not used for the GLMM, and all likelihood-based model comparisons below were therefore also estimated by maximum likelihood.

### Model Comparison (Fixed-Effects Likelihood-Ratio Test)

A likelihood-ratio test was used to compare the full multilevel logistic model with the random-intercept-only null model. The full model provided a significantly better fit to the data than the null model,

$$
\chi^2(5)=362.97,\quad p<.001.
$$

The test has 5 degrees of freedom because the model contains the five predictors retained by the main analysis's backward-elimination procedure.
